"ABSTRACT:
Existing direct position determination (DPD) methods for moving radiation sources based on time difference of arrival (TDOA) and frequency difference of arrival (FDOA) typically assume synchronous sensor networks, rendering them unsuitable for asynchronous networks affected by clock and frequency biases. To address this limitation and extend applicability to large-scale sensor networks, this paper proposes a distributed DPD algorithm for moving sources in asynchronous sensor networks based on calibration sources. To achieve distributed global optimization of parameters including clock and frequency offsets between neighboring sensors as well as the position and velocity of the source, this study introduces a distributed multiple particle filtering (MPF) framework. Utilizing the coarse estimates provided by the distributed MPF, the algorithm then applies a diffusion-based gradient method to obtain the refined estimates. Throughout the entire process, the radiation source is regarded as an increasingly reliable calibration source. The algorithm jointly utilizes information from the radiation source and the calibration sources to estimate clock and frequency biases. Meanwhile, information exchange in the algorithm is restricted to neighboring sensors, eliminating the need for multi-hop transmission. Experimental results demonstrate consistent convergence of the estimated parameters across sensors and validate the superior performance of the proposed algorithm, even under challenging conditions of low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and limited observation duration.

I. INTRODUCTION Passive localization of moving radiation sources has gained significant research attention in recent years. This technology is a crucial function of wireless sensor networks, widely applied in electronic reconnaissance, environmental sensing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and security systems [1]–[3]. To achieve high-precision localization of moving radiation sources, sensor networks typically combine time difference of arrival (TDOA) and frequency difference of arrival (FDOA) information for localization [4]. Traditional localization approaches, known as two-step methods, perform localization in two stages. In the first stage, the TDOA and FDOA values relative to a reference node are estimated based on the signals received by the sensors [5], [6]. In the second stage, these estimated parameters are further processed to derive the target’s position estimate. Classical data processing algorithm linearizes the localization equations and obtains target velocity and position estimates using a two-step weighted least squares method [7]. Numerous other algorithms for data processing have also been proposed in [8]–[10]. However, the two-step methods do not fully leverage the correlation among received signals and incur information loss during the initial estimation of parameters, leading to significant localization errors under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) environments. To address this limitation, A. J. Weiss proposed the direct position determination (DPD) algorithm in [11]. The DPD method bypasses the intermediate estimation of localization parameters such as TDOA, while directly estimates the target position from the received signals via a one-step signal processing procedure. Specifically, the DPD algorithm constructs a cost function related to the source position and searches for its extreme point. The cost function exploits the correlation among the received signals and is commonly constructed based on the maximum likelihood (ML) criterion. The point that maximizes or minimizes the cost function within the search space corresponds to the estimate, at which the correlation among the received signals is maximized. Compared with two-step methods, the DPD algorithm achieves higher localization accuracy, especially in low SNR environments [12]–[14]. Building upon the introduced DPD algorithm, methods for direct localization or direct tracking of moving targets using TDOA and FDOA information have been proposed in recent decades. In [15], particle filter (PF) was utilized to implement direct tracking of moving targets based on TDOA and FDOA information. To enable scalability for large-scale sensor networks, [16] proposed a distributed particle filtering approach for distributed direct tracking, thereby reducing the computational and communication burdens on individual sensors. In practical scenarios, the source signal may be intermittent, rendering these methods unsuitable for single-shot localization applications. Addressing the single-shot localization scenario, [17] employed the Gaussian-Newton (GN) method to iteratively estimate the source position from a single set of measurements. While well-suited for single-shot localization, the GN method is highly sensitive to the initial value and may become trapped in local optima if the initial guess is unsuitable, resulting in large localization errors. To address the challenge of global optimization, a multiple particle filtering (MPF) method was introduced in [4]. This approach not only ensures global solutions but also employs two interacting PFs that separately optimize the source’s position and velocity, decomposing the search space into two lower-dimensional subspaces. This division significantly reduces the number of particles required and lowers the computational complexity compared with traditional PF methods. The aforementioned algorithms assume the use of synchronous sensor networks for direct localization of moving targets. However, in the absence of devices such as the global positioning system (GPS) for time synchronization, clock biases commonly exist among sensors and the sensor network is asynchronous. When localizing targets using asynchronous sensor networks, it has been demonstrated in [18] that uncorrected clock biases can cause substantial localization errors. To address this, the authors proposed a DPD algorithm based on calibration sources. This approach first obtains initial estimates of the target position and clock biases via the expectationmaximization (EM) algorithm, and then refines these estimates using the GN method. In [19], the impact of time synchronization errors was mitigated by repeatedly changing the sensor positions and performing multiple observations of the target. However, both of these methods focus exclusively on localizing stationary targets and consider only TDOA information. When the frequency shifts caused by the Doppler effect are not taken into account, significant localization errors may occur for high-speed moving targets. Moreover, neither approach addresses the issue of frequency biases. In sensor networks, each sensor uses its local oscillator to down-convert the received signals. Due to factors such as manufacturing variations and temperature-induced oscillator drift, frequency offsets arise among the received baseband signals from different sensors [20], [21]. These frequency biases can adversely affect both position and velocity estimation of sources. Therefore, to achieve high-precision localization, it is essential to calibrate both the clock and frequency biases across the sensors [22], [23]. This paper thus focuses on the problem of localizing moving radiation sources using asynchronous sensor networks subject to both time and frequency synchronization errors. To overcome the inherent drawbacks of centralized processing, such as limited system robustness and the high communication bandwidth and computational demands placed on the fusion center [24]–[26], we propose a distributed DPD algorithm. The algorithm is designed to estimate a high-dimensional parameter formed by clock and frequency biases as well as source’s position and velocity. The estimation of clock and frequency biases is achieved by leveraging calibration sources with known positions and velocities but unknown transmitted signals. To address the challenge of distributed global optimization in the high dimensional parameter space, we introduce a distributed MPF method based on the diffusion strategy in [26]–[28]. By decomposing the search space and enabling interaction among PFs as well as local fusion among sensors, this approach effectively reduces the required number of particles and achieves globally consistent estimation. For further improvement of localization accuracy, the output of the distributed MPF is utilized as the initialization for subsequent processing, which employs the diffusion strategy and the gradient method to refine estimates toward consistent and accurate results. Unlike the distributed DPD methods in [19], [25], and [29], which require multi-hop transmissions and global data fusion, the proposed algorithm only necessitates information exchange between neighboring sensors, eliminating the need for storage and forwarding. Each sensor processes only local information, and consistent convergence across the network is achieved through the diffusion strategy. Consequently, the algorithm is wellsuited for application in large-scale sensor networks. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: •The scenario of distributed localization of moving sources in asynchronous sensor networks with both clock and frequency biases is modeled. Calibration sources are utilized to correct clock and frequency biases. For this setting, the local and global cost functions based on the ML criterion are proposed. The Crame ́r-Rao lower bound (CRLB) for this scenario is also derived, which is distinct from the results provided in [4], [15], and [18]. •A fully distributed DPD algorithm is developed to localize moving radiation sources in asynchronous sensor networks based on the constructed cost functions. This algorithm utilizes the proposed distributed MPF method to obtain reliable initial estimates, which are then refined using a diffusion-based gradient approach. All sensors in the network achieve consistent convergence across the estimated parameters. Throughout the entire process, information is exchanged only between neighboring sensors, and local fusion is performed, thereby eliminating the need for multi-hop transmission and centralized processing. •The impact of clock and frequency biases on localization is analyzed both theoretically and numerically. CONCLUSION This paper addressed the problem of direct localization of moving sources in asynchronous sensor networks, which are subject to both time and frequency synchronization errors. A distributed algorithm that leverages calibration sources for synchronization was proposed. The algorithm first obtains coarse estimates of clock biases, frequency biases, and the position and velocity of the radiation source using the proposed distributed MPF method. Subsequently, refined estimates are obtained at each sensor through a diffusion-based gradient method. The proposed distributed MPF achieves global optimization with a relatively small number of particles by enabling interactions among PFs within each sensor and local fusion among neighboring sensors. This provides reliable initial values for the subsequent fine estimation stage. Throughout the entire processing, information is shared via single-hop transmissions between neighboring sensors and fused locally, making the algorithm wellsuited for large-scale sensor networks. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed algorithm achieves consistent convergence across the entire sensor network and maintains robustness even under low SNR environments and limited observation durations.
